design_detail: Record-review comparison of two case definitions of a heroin-related death, applied to the same records of Maryland's statewide Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) for overdose deaths in 2012–2015. Standard approach: the death certificate's cause-of-death section contains the word 'heroin'. Enhanced surveillance (a protocol developed by the state Vital Statistics Administration, the OCME, the Maryland Poison Center and the Behavioral Health Administration): every OCME record with an intoxication-type cause-of-death term was reviewed (cause of death, toxicology results, scene-investigation notes) and counted as heroin-related if (1) heroin was on the certificate, (2) toxicology found 6-monoacetylmorphine, (3) toxicology found quinine with morphine or free morphine, or (4) the certificate named morphine or no specific substance and scene notes suggested heroin; deaths whose scene notes suggested prescription morphine were not counted. The enhanced count contains the standard count by construction. Descriptive counts, percentages and 95% confidence intervals by year, age, race or ethnicity and gender; no statistical tests.
can_establish: How many more Maryland overdose deaths in 2012–2015 met a broader protocol definition of heroin-related death (certificate wording plus toxicology markers and scene evidence) than had heroin written on the certificate, how that gap changed over the four years, and in which age, sex and racial or ethnic groups certificates named heroin least often.
cannot_establish: That the 1,052 additional deaths were caused by heroin (two of the four criteria count heroin markers found in toxicology whatever the certifier concluded; no independent reference standard was used, and who reviewed the records, or whether a second reviewer checked them, is not reported); whether any certificate naming heroin was wrong (the comparison can only add deaths); how the protocol would perform in other states or with later toxicology; or the size of the national undercount.

sample.recruitment: Records: the Maryland OCME, which must investigate every death in the state from violence, suicide or casualty, or that occurs in a suspicious, unexpected or unusual manner; cause-of-death information for 2012–2015 was provided by the OCME to the Vital Statistics Administration, which compiles the state's overdose statistics (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Standard approach: certificates of overdose deaths whose cause-of-death section includes 'heroin'. Enhanced approach: all OCME records whose cause of death includes any of poisoning, intoxication, toxicity, inhalation, ingestion, overdose, exposure, chemical, use, combined effects, combined toxic effects or effects (Methods, 3rd paragraph). The definition of the 3,957 'total overdose deaths' (intent, codes, whether alcohol-only deaths count) is not stated beyond a reference to the state's report on drug- and alcohol-related intoxication deaths (ref 7).
sample.demographics: Of the 2,182 deaths heroin-related by enhanced surveillance (Table 3): 1,680 men, 501 women; 1,505 non-Hispanic White, 623 non-Hispanic Black, 26 Hispanic, 25 other; aged under 25: 237, 25–34: 566, 35–44: 447, 45–54: 592, 55 or older: 339. No demographics are given for the 3,957 overdose deaths.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. One decedent of unknown age, 3 of unknown race and 1 of unknown gender are left out of the subgroup rows of Table 3.
sample.selection_effects: One state with a centralized, statewide medical examiner system, 2012–2015. The protocol was designed and applied by the agencies that certify the deaths and compile the official counts. The undefined denominator of overdose deaths limits comparison of the shares with other places.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count and who decided. Standard: an OCME medical certifier wrote the cause of death, described as the certifier's best medical opinion that may vary among certifiers (Methods, 1st paragraph); the count is a text search of that section for 'heroin'. Enhanced: the study team reviewed each record against the four criteria (the paper does not say who reviewed, how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the certificate, or how often they agreed). What was tested: a 'toxicology screen' recording 6-monoacetylmorphine, morphine or free morphine, and quinine, which the authors describe as a common heroin adulterant (Methods, 5th paragraph); the panel, the specimens and the share of deaths tested are not reported. Scene evidence counted as strongly suggesting heroin included reports that the person was known to use heroin and was found with drug paraphernalia, or that heroin use was witnessed on the day of death.
exposure.polysubstance: Not separated. A death counted as heroin-related whatever other drugs were present or written on the certificate, and no breakdown of co-occurring drugs is given. 55 of the additional deaths had a substance other than heroin or morphine as the certified cause; the authors concede the certifier may have judged heroin present but not directly related to the death (Discussion › Limitations).

comparison.controls: The same records classified two ways. Because criterion 1 of the enhanced approach is the standard approach, the enhanced count can only equal or exceed it. No independent reference standard (for example blinded review by forensic pathologists) was used for either approach.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Reasons certifiers did not write 'heroin' (time from use to specimen, route, chronic use, quality of analysis, morphine as heroin's breakdown product) are discussed in the Introduction, not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Counts and percentages of heroin-related deaths by approach and year (Table 1); sources of identification for the additional deaths (Table 2); the number of enhanced-approach deaths with heroin on the certificate, with percentage and 95% confidence interval, by year, age, race or ethnicity and gender (Table 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither approach was validated against an independent standard; no inter-rater reliability is reported for the judgments made from scene notes.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Heroin-related' means heroin written in the cause-of-death section (standard) or meeting any of the four criteria (enhanced). The paper uses the same words for both, although criteria 2 and 3 rest on substances found in toxicology rather than on a judgment that heroin caused the death.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests; subgroup differences are described from percentages and confidence intervals.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The review was done within the agencies that produce the counts, and the chief medical examiner is a co-author.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heroin-related deaths 2012–2015: 1,130 by certificates against 2,182 by enhanced surveillance (1.93 times as many, editors' calculation), 28.6% against 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths. By year: 2012, 179 against 392 (22.4% and 49.1% of 799); 2013, 221 against 464 (25.8% and 54.1% of 858); 2014, 309 against 578 (29.7% and 55.5% of 1,041); 2015, 421 against 748 (33.4% and 59.4% of 1,259). Share of enhanced-approach deaths with heroin on the certificate: 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) overall, rising from 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 58.2% under age 25 falling to 41.9% at 55 or older; non-Hispanic White 53.5%, non-Hispanic Black 47.0%; men 56.8%, women 35.1%; non-Hispanic Black women 25.9% (18.5 to 33.3); Hispanic men 77.3% (17 of 22); Hispanic women 0 of 4. Of the 1,052 additional deaths, the certificate named morphine for 804 (76.4%), no specific substance for 193 (18.3%) and another substance for 55 (5.2%); toxicology showed 6-monoacetylmorphine in 136, morphine with quinine in 892, and morphine or free morphine in 998 (overlapping). Editors' calculation: the 1,052 additional deaths are 26.6% of all 3,957 overdose deaths, and certificates named heroin in 52% of protocol-defined heroin deaths.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; no ethics approval was needed because the study involved only deceased individuals (Human Participant Protection).
analysis.selective_reporting: No breakdown of the additional deaths by the criterion, or combination of criteria, that qualified them; Table 2's sources overlap and do not sum to 1,052, and one of its rows conflicts with the text (reporting issue 1).
analysis.power: Not applicable. Subgroup intervals are wide for Hispanic and 'other' groups (22 to 26 deaths), and there is none for Hispanic women (4 deaths).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Applying a broader protocol to the same Maryland medical-examiner records, 2,182 overdose deaths in 2012–2015 met at least one heroin criterion, against 1,130 with 'heroin' written on the certificate. Most of the 1,052 extra deaths had morphine certified as the cause together with scene evidence of heroin, toxicology markers (6-monoacetylmorphine in 136; morphine with quinine in 892) or both. The share of protocol-defined heroin deaths that the certificates named rose from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015 and was lowest for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), women (35.1%) and Black women (25.9%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says certificates "may underestimate the contribution of heroin", which the data support. The Limitations go further: the enhanced approach "almost certainly provides a more accurate count", asserted without any reference standard. Gaps: (1) the enhanced definition contains the standard one, so 'nearly double' measures how much broader it is, not how often certificates are wrong, and the design cannot detect certificates that name heroin wrongly; (2) two criteria rest on toxicology presence, and the 55 deaths certified as due to another substance were counted even though the certifier may have judged heroin present but not causal, so 'heroin-related' in the enhanced count partly means 'heroin present'; (3) the Discussion's statements that certificates underestimate heroin deaths among older people, women and Black people, and that enhanced counts were substantially higher among Hispanic women, rest on percentages without tests and, for Hispanic women, on 4 deaths; (4) the Public Health Implications suggest that recent rises in deaths attributed to heart disease might be missed overdose deaths, with no data in the paper; (5) the linked editorial (Galea and Vaughan, 2018) repeats the finding as showing that enhanced surveillance can better identify heroin, without noting the missing reference standard; (6) the Discussion (8th paragraph) presents the rise in the share named on certificates, from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, as a sign that the recommendations are being implemented in Maryland, without any data on when or how they were implemented, so a trend over time is read as an effect.

timeline.event: SAMHSA consensus panel recommends uniform standards and case definitions for opioid-related deaths (ref 10, cited with ref 11 in the Discussion, 6th paragraph, for the need for standardized methods); the recommendations summarized in the 7th paragraph, including naming the parent drug rather than the metabolite when evidence supports it, are attributed to SAMHSA experts but printed with ref 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report, presumably meant as ref 10

Mertz, Janssen and Williams (Journal of Forensic Sciences): heroin under-represented among unintentional overdose deaths in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, when morphine was certified (ref 6); a similar county case review.

Slavova et al., 'let's get specific': in 2010 the overdose death rate attributed to other and unspecified drugs ranged from 0.2 to 7.4 per 100,000 across 11 jurisdictions (US 3.1), as cited in this paper's Discussion (ref 4)

Galea and Vaughan, issue editorial in the American Journal of Public Health (doi 10.2105/AJPH.2018.304422, PMC5944893), linked from this article: summarizes it as showing that standard certificates may underestimate heroin deaths and that enhanced surveillance can better identify them; no critique of the method.
Buchanich et al.: national reallocation of unintentional overdose deaths with no named drug; a different approach to undercounting, on national certificates (card sc_buchanich_2018)

Gutkind et al. scoping review: summarizes this study as 1,052 additional heroin-related deaths, 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths in Maryland 2012–2015, and places it beside county reviews in New York City (heroin deaths +17%), San Francisco and Allegheny County and a 38-state SUDORS analysis that all found heroin under-named on certificates (card sc_gutkind_2025)

replication.where_it_stands: The direction agrees with case reviews elsewhere summarized by Gutkind et al. (2025): heroin is under-named on certificates, mostly because morphine is written instead. The size varies widely (about 17% more heroin deaths in New York City and 13–21% in San Francisco, as Gutkind et al. report them, against nearly double here), and none of the studies read for this round checks either approach against an independent standard, or in both directions. Maryland's own certificates named heroin more often each year of the study (45.7% to 56.3%), which the authors link to the recommendations being implemented, without data on implementation.

funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement appears on the PMC page.
funding.affiliations_note: At the time of the study, Horon, Singal and Sharfstein were with the Maryland Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, Baltimore, which compiles the state's overdose statistics; Fowler is the chief medical examiner of the State of Maryland, whose office wrote the certificates evaluated; correspondence to Sharfstein at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. The study evaluates the authors' own agencies' data with a protocol those agencies developed; recorded as a flag for closer reading. By the CONTRIBUTORS note (author information), Fowler contributed to the study's conceptualization and design, to data collection and to revision, and Horon to conceptualization and design, data collection, analysis and interpretation, so the certifying office took part in designing the comparison as well as in supplying the records.

what_would_settle_it: Blinded review of a random sample of both groups of Maryland records (the 1,130 certificates naming heroin and the 1,052 added deaths) by forensic pathologists outside the office, using a written causal standard and the toxicology concentrations and scene evidence, reporting agreement with each approach in both directions; repeated in states with coroner systems.

domains.note: The statewide medical examiner must investigate unexpected and unusual deaths, so its records are the right frame for Maryland overdose deaths.
All records with intoxication-type cause-of-death terms, 2012–2015; no sampling.
3,957 overdose deaths and 2,182 protocol-defined heroin deaths; small subgroups (Hispanic, other; 4 Hispanic women) are imprecise.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics of the heroin-related deaths and the setting are described; the definition of the 3,957 overdose deaths and the toxicology panel are not.

domains.note: 6-monoacetylmorphine is a specific heroin marker and morphine with quinine a presumptive one; but the protocol was never validated, scene-note judgments are subjective, and criteria 2 and 3 count presence, not a judgment of cause.

domains.note: One written protocol, but who applied it, whether reviewers were blind to the certificate and how consistently it was applied are not reported; the standard approach depends on individual certifiers' wording, which the authors say varies.

Counts, percentages and 95% confidence intervals are appropriate and re-derive from the tables; Wald-type intervals are given for subgroups of 22 to 26 deaths, no interval for 4, and subgroup differences are interpreted without tests.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths from a state register compared under two case definitions (round brief, certificate studies). The comparison is in effect a check of the certificates' sensitivity against a broader definition, but the broader definition is not a validated reference: it includes the certificates by construction, rests partly on presence in toxicology and on unblinded scene-note judgments, and was built and applied by the agencies that produce the counts. Counts and percentages are internally consistent, apart from one table row. Citable for: in Maryland 2012–2015, certificates named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths while 2,182 met a protocol combining certificate wording, toxicology markers and scene evidence; most missed cases had morphine written as the cause; certificates named heroin less often for older people, women and Black women; the share named rose from 45.7% to 56.3%. Not citable for: heroin as the cause of all 2,182 deaths, the accuracy of certificates that name heroin, or undercounting outside Maryland.

key_findings.finding: Maryland 2012–2015: death certificates naming heroin identified 1,130 heroin-related overdose deaths; enhanced surveillance identified 2,182, nearly double; that is 28.6% against 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths.

By year, certificates against enhanced surveillance: 2012, 179 (22.4% of 799) against 392 (49.1%); 2013, 221 (25.8% of 858) against 464 (54.1%); 2014, 309 (29.7% of 1,041) against 578 (55.5%); 2015, 421 (33.4% of 1,259) against 748 (59.4%). Overdose deaths, heroin-related deaths and the heroin share all rose over the period by both approaches.

Enhanced-surveillance criteria: heroin on the certificate; 6-monoacetylmorphine in toxicology; quinine with morphine or free morphine in toxicology; or morphine or no specific substance on the certificate plus scene notes suggesting heroin. Deaths with scene notes suggesting prescription morphine were not counted. The protocol was developed by the Vital Statistics Administration, the OCME, the Maryland Poison Center and the Behavioral Health Administration.

Of the 1,052 additional deaths, the certificate named morphine, alone or with other substances, for 804 (76.4%), gave no specific substance (for example narcotic or opioid intoxication) for 193 (18.3%) and named another substance for 55 (5.2%). Every record certifying morphine had scene evidence suggesting heroin.
key_findings.note: Table 2 gives 1,042 for morphine certified with scene evidence; the text's 804 is consistent with 804 + 193 + 55 = 1,052 (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Sources for the additional deaths (overlapping): toxicology showed 6-monoacetylmorphine in 136 records, morphine with quinine in 892, and morphine or free morphine in 998.

Among the 2,182 protocol-defined heroin deaths, the certificate named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9), rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015; by age, 58.2% under 25, 58.0% at 25–34, 54.6% at 35–44, 47.0% at 45–54 and 41.9% at 55 or older.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Total, Year of death, Age group rows); RESULTS, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: By sex and race or ethnicity, the certificate named heroin in 56.8% of deaths of men and 35.1% of women; non-Hispanic White 53.5%, non-Hispanic Black 47.0%; non-Hispanic White men 57.9%, women 39.4%; non-Hispanic Black men 52.9%, women 25.9% (18.5 to 33.3); Hispanic men 77.3% (17 of 22), Hispanic women 0 of 4.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (Race/ethnicity, Gender, Race/ethnicity and gender rows); RESULTS, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: With enhanced surveillance the largest number of heroin-related deaths was at ages 45–54 (592) rather than 25–34 (566), whereas by certificates the peak was at 25–34 (328 against 278 at 45–54).

Who certifies: the OCME must investigate all Maryland deaths from violence, suicide or casualty, or that are suspicious, unexpected or unusual; the cause of death it writes is the certifier's best medical opinion and may vary among certifiers. The authors judge the office's approach possibly conservative in attributing deaths to heroin.

Why certificates miss heroin, as the authors give it: certifiers may write a nonspecific cause such as narcotic intoxication or drug overdose; time from use to specimen, route, chronic use and quality of analysis make identification hard; heroin itself is rarely detected because of its short half-life, so its breakdown products morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine are found and morphine intoxication may be written.

The authors' own limitation, in the overcounting direction: some deaths counted by enhanced surveillance may not have been heroin-related, including some certified as morphine intoxication, and some of the 55 deaths certified as due to another substance, where the certifier may have judged heroin present but not directly related; they judge these few.

Recommendations cited from SAMHSA experts: list every physiologically significant drug, name the parent drug rather than the metabolite when toxicology or scene findings support it (for example heroin rather than morphine), avoid the terms 'overdose' and 'use' on certificates, and evaluate whether toxicology can distinguish chronic from acute use.
key_findings.note: The paragraph's citation is reference 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report; the SAMHSA consensus panel paper (Goldberger et al. 2013) is reference 10, cited with reference 11 in the paragraph before, so the citation is probably misnumbered (reporting issue 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The text twice gives 804 additional records that certified morphine as the cause (76.4% of 1,052, with 193 and 55 making up the rest), while Table 2 gives 1,042 in its row for morphine listed as the cause on the certificate with supporting scene evidence.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, RESULTS, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: 1,042 would leave only 10 of the 1,052 additional deaths without morphine on the certificate, contradicting the 193 and 55 in the text; use 804.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's third toxicology row reads 'morphine or free morphine and supporting evidence from scene investigation' (998), while the text describes the 998 as records showing morphine or free morphine, with no scene condition. Neither matches the four criteria in the Methods, in which morphine in toxicology counts only with quinine, or through a certificate naming morphine or no substance plus scene notes. The abstract likewise names morphine 'alone' as a major factor.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2; RESULTS, 2nd paragraph; METHODS, 4th paragraph; Abstract › Results
reporting_issues.consequence: How many additional deaths each criterion qualified, alone or together, cannot be reconstructed; morphine in toxicology without quinine, 6-monoacetylmorphine or scene evidence was not, by the Methods, enough to count a death.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominator of 3,957 'total overdose deaths' is not defined (intent, ICD-10 codes, whether alcohol-only intoxications are included); the Methods cite the state report on drug- and alcohol-related intoxication deaths for the cause-of-death terms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 28.6% and 55.1% shares, and Gutkind et al.'s restatement of the additional deaths as 26% of all drug-related overdose deaths, have an undefined denominator; the counts of heroin deaths are not affected.

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries no funding statement and no conflict-of-interest statement on the PMC page; the authors include the state's chief medical examiner and officials of the health department whose data are evaluated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, whole article; Author information
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding and interests cannot be recorded; the institutional link is noted in the affiliations.

reporting_issues.issue: DISCUSSION, 7th paragraph attributes recommendations to experts of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (list every physiologically significant drug, name the parent drug rather than the metabolite, avoid 'overdose' and 'use', evaluate whether toxicology can separate chronic from acute use) but cites reference 12, the 2015 Maryland Vital Statistics Annual Report; the SAMHSA consensus panel paper is reference 10, cited with reference 11 in the 6th paragraph.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, DISCUSSION, 6th and 7th paragraphs; References 10 to 12
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misnumbered citation; the recommendations should be traced to Goldberger et al. (2013; reference 10, card sc_goldberger_2013), not to the state report.

reporting_issues.issue: RESULTS, 3rd paragraph describes the Table 3 percentages as the percentage of overdose death records reporting heroin, and Table 3 heads them 'Identified Through Standard Surveillance'; they are the share of protocol-defined heroin deaths (the enhanced count, Table 3's Total column) whose certificate named heroin, not a share of all overdose deaths.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, RESULTS, 3rd paragraph; Table 3, column headings
reporting_issues.consequence: They measure the certificates' sensitivity against the broader definition. The card's findings use the right denominator; the paper's wording should not be copied into claims.
